title: The scheduler and StartNew
cards/0/body:
A task that has a delegate does not start itself. It is handed to a task scheduler (TaskScheduler), which decides where and when to run it:

  • TaskScheduler.Default — the thread pool;
  • FromCurrentSynchronizationContext() — into the current context, for example the UI thread;
  • ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair — a ready-made pair for limits: "no more than N at once" and "strictly one at a time".

Tasks from async methods and TaskCompletionSource have no delegate: they are not run but completed from outside (as in unit 1). They need no scheduler.
cards/0/deep:
A custom scheduler derives from TaskScheduler and implements three methods: QueueTask (accept a task), TryExecuteTaskInline (may it run right now on this thread) and GetScheduledTasks (for the debugger).

Inlining happens, for example, on Wait() for a task that has not started yet: the waiting thread may run it itself instead of standing idle. One more detail: if there is no SynchronizationContext and TaskScheduler.Current is not Default, await resumes on that scheduler. Code under a ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair stays under it after await.
cards/1/q: Which task never goes through a TaskScheduler at all?
cards/1/options/0: A task returned by an async method
cards/1/explain: An async method's task is a promise without a delegate: the state machine builder completes it. The other three carry a delegate, and someone has to run it — that is exactly the scheduler's job.
cards/2/title: Task.Run is StartNew with the right settings
cards/2/body:
Task.Run arrived in .NET 4.5 as a shorthand for the most common case. It equals StartNew with three explicit decisions: no token, no child attachment, strictly the pool. And for an async lambda it also does Unwrap.

A "bare" Task.Factory.StartNew(work) differs in everything: scheduler Current (the trap from the last lesson), options None, no unwrapping.

You need StartNew when you need what it offers: a custom scheduler, LongRunning, a state object without a closure.
cards/3/options/3: Does not compile: StartNew does not accept an async lambda
cards/3/explain: StartNew returned Task<Task>. The outer task completed when the lambda reached its first await and returned the inner task. await waited only for that. With Task.Run it would be about 1000.
cards/4/body:
Creation options are hints for the scheduler and rules for task relationships:

  • LongRunning — work that takes a long time. The default scheduler gives it a dedicated thread instead of a pool thread: the pool keeps its worker and does not have to wait to inject new threads;
  • PreferFairness — into the pool's global queue rather than the current thread's local queue: closer to first come, first served;
  • AttachedToParent and DenyChildAttach — task relationships, more on them below;
  • HideScheduler — inside the task TaskScheduler.Current looks like Default;
  • RunContinuationsAsynchronously — as with TaskCompletionSource in unit 5.
cards/4/deep:
In the default scheduler LongRunning is literal: it creates new Thread(…) { IsBackground = true }, which runs one task and exits. Creating a thread means an OS object and a stack reservation, on the order of tens of microseconds or more. For short tasks the option hurts.

It is only a hint: a custom scheduler may ignore it. And with an async lambda the dedicated thread lives only until the first real pause.
cards/5/q: How long does the dedicated thread allocated for LongRunning live?
cards/5/options/0: Until the first real pause at an await
cards/5/options/1: As long as the loop spins, i.e. forever
cards/5/options/2: Not at all: the option fails with an async lambda
cards/5/options/3: Until the garbage collector collects the task
cards/5/explain: The delegate is an async lambda. At the first incomplete await it returns a task, and the thread is free — so it exits. The loop continues on pool threads. The dedicated thread was created for nothing. This loop does not need LongRunning: it does not hold a thread anyway.
cards/6/body:
A task created inside a running task with AttachedToParent becomes its child:

  • the parent does not complete until all its children have. While it waits, its status is WaitingForChildrenToComplete;
  • children's exceptions end up in the parent's AggregateException.

Without the option a nested task is independent (detached): the parent knows nothing about it.

This is the "structured parallelism" model of .NET 4.0. New code does the same explicitly: collect the tasks and wait with WhenAll.
cards/6/deep: How it works: on creation a task checks which task is currently running on this thread. If AttachedToParent is set and that task has no DenyChildAttach, the parent's counter of unfinished children goes up. When the parent finishes its delegate, it decrements the counter for itself; each child decrements it on completion. Zero means the parent is complete.
cards/7/explain: The child is attached: Wait on the parent waits for it too. "parent" prints at once, "child" after 500 ms, and only then is the parent complete and "done" printed.
cards/8/body:
Whether to attach is decided by the child, that is, by someone else's code. Imagine a library inside your Task.Run creates a task with AttachedToParent. Your task suddenly waits for foreign work and receives foreign exceptions — and you never asked for that.

DenyChildAttach on the parent silently cancels such requests: the child becomes an ordinary independent task, without any error. Task.Run always sets it.
cards/9/q: In the code from the previous exercise the outer StartNew was replaced with Task.Run. What changes?
cards/9/options/0: done prints before child: the child does not attach
cards/9/options/1: Nothing: the child's option beats the parent's settings
cards/9/options/3: child never prints: the child task gets cancelled
cards/9/explain: Task.Run sets DenyChildAttach, and the child's AttachedToParent is silently ignored. Wait covers only the parent body: "parent", "done", and "child" after 500 ms if the process is still alive.
cards/10/q: Hardware polling is a blocking loop that runs for hours. Give it a dedicated thread without touching the pool, strictly through the standard scheduler
cards/10/explain: LongRunning with the default scheduler gives a dedicated thread. Default so as not to depend on which task the code is called from.
cards/11/options/1: Task.Factory.StartNew without a scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current
cards/11/options/2: Task.Run unwraps the Task<Task> from an async lambda
cards/11/options/3: LongRunning guarantees a dedicated thread with any scheduler
cards/11/options/4: PreferFairness makes a task run faster
cards/11/explain: LongRunning is a hint: only the default scheduler turns it into a dedicated thread. PreferFairness changes the queue, not the speed.
cards/12/q: Match the option to its effect
cards/12/pairs/0/1: A dedicated thread instead of the pool
cards/12/pairs/1/1: The global queue instead of the local one
cards/12/pairs/2/1: The parent waits for this child
